If then Jesus is He who is to come, and if, after His coming,
the world is renewed for the man who allows his being to be
transformed by the Saviour, then we have also the answer
to our other question: how can we, after He has come, still
speak of Him as the One who is to come?
Just because through His coming, our outlook on the
world and on time is completely changed. The event of His
coming is not an event within the process of world history,
an event such as is straightway merged with the past; it is
rather an event which signifies the end of the process of world
history. Those who believe in the One who is to come are
lifted out of the flux of time into the transcendence of
eternity; they have truth, purity, and fullness of life; as pain
and death have no further power to reduce them to despair,
so the evil around them and within them can no longer
make them afraid. It is engulfed in the full tide of divine
grace.
Faith gives to the Christian this unshakable certitude.
And it is the characteristic situation of Christians that so
long as they remain on earth they must walk by faith, not
sight. They who in Christ are made victorious over the world
of time, nevertheless still remain immersed in that world.
And just because the coming of Jesus is not merely an event
taking its place in past history, but an event which spells the
end of all history, for them the One who has come is always
at the same time the One who is to come and will be so to
the end of the world and of time. For ourselves who still
are implicated in the process of world history, He is always
the One who is to come, always the One who ever anew
enables us to transcend the flux and vicissitudes of time, with
its sorrow and sin and death.
Thus He confronts us always as the One who is to come,
